problem: 'relative weakness' reduced to 'how weak'; the comparison with the States is lost.
replacement: This was a heavy blow to the independence of the States. They were now bound not only by the laws but by the interpretation of the laws: by one limit that was known and another that was uncertain, by a rule that was fixed and another that was arbitrary. The Constitution did lay down the exact limits of Federal supremacy, yet whenever a State disputes that supremacy, a Federal tribunal rules on the question. Still, the threat this arrangement posed to the independence of the States is less serious than it looks. We shall see later that in America the true strength of the country lies far more in the State governments than in the Federal government. The Federal judges are aware of the relative weakness of the power in whose name they act. They are readier to give up a claim of jurisdiction that is rightfully theirs than to press a privilege they have no legal title to.

problem: Added enumerators 'first' and 'second' where the source has 'on the one hand ... on the other'.
replacement: Having provided the means of fixing the competence of the Federal courts, the legislators of the Union defined the cases that should fall within their jurisdiction. They established, on the one hand, that certain parties must always be brought before the Federal courts, whatever the special nature of the case; and, on the other, that certain kinds of cases must always be brought before those same courts, whatever the standing of the parties to the suit. These distinctions were thus accepted as the basis of Federal jurisdiction.

problem: Hedge 'we shall be led to acknowledge ... when we recollect' flattened into a flat assertion, and 'always' dropped ('have always rather exaggerated').
replacement: The present Constitution of the Union was drawn up later than those of most of the States, and it may have benefited from what experience had taught by then. But we shall be led to acknowledge that this is only a secondary cause of its superiority, when we recall that eleven new States *n have joined the American Confederation since the Federal Constitution was promulgated, and that these new republics have always rather exaggerated the defects of the earlier Constitutions than avoided them.

problem: 'it may at least represent' became 'it would at least stand for' (modal sharpened) and the hypothetical 'if' recast as 'even if'; 'The aim was' added.
replacement: The Federal Constitution, like the Constitutions of the individual States, divided the legislative body into two branches. In the States, however, both branches were made up of the same elements and chosen in the same way. As a result the passions and moods of the populace were voiced as quickly and as forcefully in one chamber as in the other, and laws were made in a violent and hasty manner. Under the Federal Constitution the two houses also come from the choice of the people, but the requirements for eligibility and the method of election were changed, so that if one branch of the legislature represents the same interests as the other, as is the case in certain nations, it may at least represent a higher degree of intelligence and discretion. A mature age was made a requirement for a senator, and the upper house was chosen by an elected assembly with a limited number of members.
